title: Writing Non-Fiction
description: Crafting real-world texts — formal letters, newspaper reports, speeches, travel articles and autobiography, with control of formality and argument.

notes.heading: Register: Formal and Informal Writing
notes.body: Register is the level of formality you choose, and it must match your audience and purpose. Formal register: no contractions (write 'do not', 'cannot'), no slang or text-speak, precise vocabulary, complete sentences, and often impersonal constructions ('It is recommended that...' rather than 'I reckon...'). Use it for essays, official letters, reports, applications and newspaper journalism. Informal register: contractions, colloquial language, direct address, humour and a conversational feel — right for messages to friends, personal blogs, postcards and anecdotes. Where formal writing appears: essays, textbooks, official letters, contracts, instruction manuals. Where informal appears: social media posts, comic books, personal blogs. Common pitfall: drifting between registers mid-text ('Furthermore, the new policy is well dodgy') — pick a register at the planning stage and hold it. Exam tip: when a task names the audience (headteacher, local council, newspaper editor), that is your register cue — assume formal unless told otherwise.

notes.heading: Building an Argument with Connectives
notes.body: A convincing argument paragraph has three moving parts: a topic sentence stating the point, a supporting statement (a fact, statistic, example or expert quotation), and a sentence explaining how the support proves the point. Sequence your paragraphs so the strongest points come early, and anticipate the obvious objection rather than ignoring it: 'Critics argue that...; however, ...' Connectives are the glue between sentences and paragraphs, and the right one depends on the relationship between ideas: addition — 'furthermore', 'moreover'; contrast — 'however', 'whereas', 'on the other hand'; cause and effect — 'therefore', 'as a result', 'consequently'; sequence and conclusion — 'firstly', 'finally', 'in conclusion'. Choosing the wrong connective reverses your meaning: 'It rained, therefore the match continued' is nonsense where 'It rained; however, the match continued' makes sense. Pitfalls: stacking 'and... and... and', or beginning every sentence with 'Also'. For the full rhetorical toolkit (emotive language, rule of three, direct address), see the Persuasive & Argumentative Writing topic — this one is about the skeleton those techniques hang on.

notes.heading: Planning, Drafting and Redrafting
notes.body: A plan is a thinking space, not a finished product — nobody marks it, so crossings-out and half-formed ideas are allowed and expected. Match the tool to the task: a mind map generates and connects ideas quickly; a bullet list orders points by importance or chronology; a flow chart sequences events or steps. Always plan around three things — purpose, audience and form. Then write a fast first draft: follow the plan, tick items off as you use them, and do not stop to fix spelling or hunt for the perfect word — quality comes later. Re-read the task before each new paragraph to stop yourself drifting off topic. Redraft in three passes: annotate (mark up the draft with changes and additions), rewrite (produce a cleaner version, upgrading word choice and tightening sentences), proofread (a final check for spelling, punctuation and grammar). Reading your work aloud catches clumsy phrasing your eye skips over. Exam tip: in a 20-minute timed task, two or three minutes on a quick bullet plan saves more time than it costs — an unplanned answer usually stalls or wanders.

notes.heading: Formal Letters: Layout and Language
notes.body: Formal letters follow fixed layout conventions, and getting them right is an easy way to earn credit. Your own address goes in the top right, with the date beneath it; the recipient's name and address sit on the left, below yours. Open with 'Dear' plus the person's name if you know it ('Dear Mr Okafor'); use 'Dear Sir/Madam' only when you don't. The sign-off rule: named recipient → 'Yours sincerely'; unnamed ('Dear Sir/Madam') → 'Yours faithfully'. Paragraph one states your purpose immediately — 'I am writing to apply for...', 'I am writing to complain about...' The body keeps one clear point per paragraph in a formal register throughout: no contractions, and stay polite even when complaining ('I would be grateful if you could...' rather than 'You'd better sort this out'). The final paragraph tells the reader exactly what you want to happen next and thanks them for their time. Pitfalls: opening with 'Hi', texting abbreviations, and ending a complaint with a threat instead of a requested action.

notes.heading: Newspaper Reports
notes.body: A newspaper report has a recognisable skeleton: headline → by-line (the reporter's name, sometimes with a one-line summary) → lead paragraph → body → closing look ahead. The lead paragraph answers Who? What? Where? When? Why? in a sentence or two — a reader who stops there still knows the story. The body adds detail in roughly chronological order: facts, statistics, and quotations from witnesses or experts — quotes are the heart of a report, giving it human voice and authority. Audience shapes style. Tabloids favour short punchy sentences, informal language, and headlines built on puns, alliteration and mild exaggeration ('Baked Britain'); broadsheets run longer, more analytical articles with restrained headlines ('Hottest day of the year in UK heatwave'). Photographs are never just decoration: they steer the reader's emotional response, so choose them as deliberately as words. Pitfall: letting opinion seep into a news report — reporters report; columnists comment. Keep the facts verifiable and let quotations carry the views.

notes.heading: Speeches: Writing for the Ear
notes.body: A speech is written for the ear, not the eye — your audience cannot rewind you. Open with a hook: a surprising statistic ('up to a million species are threatened with extinction right now'), a vivid image, a rhetorical question, or a short amusing anecdote — then make your topic clear. Address the audience directly ('you') so every listener feels personally spoken to. Keep the body simple: two or three main points, most important first, in a logical order, each backed by an example, an easy-to-grasp statistic or an expert quotation — do not overload with detail. Make key points stick with repetition and the rule of three ('government of the people, by the people, for the people'), emotive vocabulary, and short sentences for punch. Alliteration adds polish in small doses. End memorably: circle back to your opening image or close with a clear call to action the audience can actually perform. Pitfall: writing paragraphs that would read well on paper but lose a live audience — if a listener would need to re-read a sentence, cut or split it.

notes.heading: Travel Articles and Autobiography
notes.body: Both are first-person non-fiction built from real experience, and both succeed by selection, not exhaustiveness. A travel article informs AND entertains: anchor the reader with concrete sensory detail (sights, sounds, smells), weave in facts about the place and its culture, and bring it alive through anecdote and a personal, chatty-but-knowledgeable voice; a loose journey structure (arrival → exploration → reflection) keeps it organised. Autobiography is the story of your own life, told by you — distinct from a biography (someone else's life, written by another person), a diary (written as events happen), and a memoir (autobiographical writing focused on one period or theme). Choose a shape: chronological from an early starting point, or open on a turning-point moment — a decision, success or unusual event — and range outward from there. Select the people, places and events that changed you and leave the boring bits out; reflect on what each experience taught you, because meaning matters more than a complete record. Write in the past tense, first person, with descriptive detail — Roald Dahl's 'Boy' covers only his school years, yet says everything about the writer he became.

flashcards.definition: The level of formality in a piece of writing, chosen to suit the audience and purpose.
flashcards.example: 'I would not recommend this' (formal) vs 'I wouldn't bother with it' (informal).

flashcards.definition: A word or phrase that links ideas between sentences or paragraphs — for addition, contrast, cause/effect or sequence.
flashcards.example: 'It rained; as a result, the match was cancelled.' Other examples: however, furthermore, firstly.

flashcards.definition: The sentence, usually first in a paragraph, that states the paragraph's main point.
flashcards.example: 'Recycling schemes benefit communities in three ways.' — the rest of the paragraph explains those ways.

flashcards.definition: Improving a first draft in three passes: annotate the draft, rewrite using those notes, then proofread.
flashcards.example: Marking weak word choices on a draft, rewriting the paragraph with stronger vocabulary, then checking spelling.

flashcards.definition: The final check of a piece of writing for spelling, punctuation and grammar errors.
flashcards.example: Reading your letter aloud and correcting 'their' to 'there' before handing it in.

flashcards.definition: The paired opening and closing of a formal letter: 'Dear + name' pairs with 'Yours sincerely'; 'Dear Sir/Madam' pairs with 'Yours faithfully'.
flashcards.example: Dear Mrs Chen ... Yours sincerely. Dear Sir or Madam ... Yours faithfully.

flashcards.definition: The line beneath a newspaper headline naming the reporter, sometimes with a one-line summary of the story.
flashcards.example: 'Amy Jones reports on how the heatwave is predicted to break records.'

flashcards.definition: The opening paragraph of a news report that answers Who? What? Where? When? Why? in a sentence or two.
flashcards.example: 'Record temperatures hit 37°C across southern England yesterday as the UK's third heatwave of the summer peaked.'

flashcards.definition: A 'serious' newspaper with in-depth, analytical articles and restrained headlines — contrasted with the more sensational, pun-loving tabloid.
flashcards.example: 'Hottest day of the year in UK heatwave' (broadsheet) vs 'Baked Britain' (tabloid).

flashcards.definition: A question asked for effect, with no answer expected — it makes an audience stop and think.
flashcards.example: 'Do we really want to be the generation that let our library close?'

flashcards.definition: A short, often amusing true story used to hook an audience or illustrate a point.
flashcards.example: Opening a speech about stage fright with the story of forgetting your lines in the school play.

flashcards.definition: Autobiographical writing that focuses on one important period or theme of the writer's life rather than their whole life story.
flashcards.example: Roald Dahl's 'Boy', which covers only his school years.

questions.stem: Which sentence is written in an appropriate register for a formal letter to a headteacher?
choices: Hiya, just wanted to moan about the new timetable, it's well annoying.
I can't believe the changes — sort it out ASAP!
I am writing to express my concern about the proposed changes to the school day.
The new timetable is a bit rubbish, to be honest.
questions.explanation: Formal register means complete sentences, precise vocabulary, no contractions ('I am', not 'I'm') and no slang. The other options fail on every count: 'Hiya', 'moan', 'well annoying', 'ASAP' and 'a bit rubbish' are all informal choices that would undermine a letter to someone in authority.

choices: A word or phrase that links ideas between sentences or paragraphs, such as 'however'
A type of punctuation used to join two independent clauses
The first sentence of a paragraph that states its main point
A quotation from an expert used to support an argument
questions.explanation: Connectives (however, therefore, furthermore, firstly) signal the relationship between ideas — contrast, cause, addition or sequence. The third option describes a topic sentence; connectives are about joining, not introducing.

questions.stem: A formal letter that opens 'Dear Sir or Madam' should end with:
choices: Yours sincerely,
Best wishes,
Love from,
Yours faithfully,
questions.explanation: The rule pairs the greeting with the sign-off: you only use 'Yours sincerely' when you have named the recipient ('Dear Mrs Chen'). 'Dear Sir/Madam' means you don't know their name, so it pairs with 'Yours faithfully'. 'Best wishes' and 'Love from' are informal closings.

questions.stem: The lead paragraph of a newspaper report should:
choices: Give the reporter's personal opinion on the events
Answer Who? What? Where? When? Why? in a sentence or two
Describe every event in full chronological detail
Hook the reader with a pun or joke
questions.explanation: The lead carries the essential facts so a reader who stops there still knows the story. Detail and chronology belong to the body; opinion belongs to columnists, not news reporters; playful headlines may hook readers, but the lead itself delivers facts.

choices: The story of someone's life written by another person
A personal record of events written as they happen
The story of your own life, written by you
A fictional story based loosely on real events
questions.explanation: 'Auto' means self: an autobiography is your life story told by you. The first option describes a biography, the second a diary. Unlike fiction, autobiography claims to be a true account — though the writer still selects which events to include.

questions.stem: You have 20 minutes for a timed writing task. What is the best use of the first few minutes?
choices: Spend 2–3 minutes on a quick bullet-point plan, then start writing
Start writing immediately — planning wastes precious time
Write a neat, detailed plan in full sentences before drafting
Write the conclusion first so you know where the piece is heading
questions.explanation: A plan is a thinking space — it doesn't need to be neat or complete, just enough to order your ideas. Two or three minutes of rough bullet points keeps the writing focused and saves far more time than it costs. A polished full-sentence plan eats writing time for no benefit; diving in with no plan usually leads to drifting off task.

questions.stem: Read this paragraph opening: 'School uniforms save families money. A single uniform costs less than a term's worth of fashion outfits, and parents avoid pressure to buy the latest brands.' Which sentence is the topic sentence?
choices: Both sentences equally — they share the role
'A single uniform costs less than a term's worth of fashion outfits'
'Parents avoid pressure to buy the latest brands'
'School uniforms save families money'
questions.explanation: The topic sentence states the paragraph's main point — here, that uniforms save money. The other two sentences are supporting statements: they give evidence and explanation that prove the point. A topic sentence is usually first and is always the most general statement in the paragraph.

questions.stem: Choose the best connective: 'The leisure centre's facilities are excellent. ___, membership fees have doubled this year.'
choices: Furthermore
However
Therefore
As a result
questions.explanation: The second clause contrasts with the first — praise followed by a criticism — so a contrast connective ('However') is needed. 'Furthermore' adds a agreeing point, while 'Therefore' and 'As a result' claim the fee rise was caused by the excellent facilities, which reverses the logic.

questions.stem: Why do speech writers often open with a surprising statistic or a rhetorical question?
choices: Because speeches are marked on statistical accuracy
To fill time while the audience settles down
To hook the audience's attention before the topic is made clear
To prove the speaker has done academic research
questions.explanation: A speech is written for the ear: if you lose the audience in the first thirty seconds, nothing after that matters. A shocking fact or a question with no expected answer makes listeners stop and think, earning their attention before you state your topic. The statistic must still be relevant and easy to grasp — it is a hook, not proof of scholarship.

questions.stem: Which headline is most typical of a tabloid newspaper covering a heatwave?
choices: 'Baked Britain Burns!'
'Hottest day of the year recorded in UK heatwave'
'Met Office issues amber weather warning for southern England'
'Temperatures reach 37°C, exceeding previous July records'
questions.explanation: Tabloids grab attention with alliteration ('Baked Britain Burns'), drama and mild exaggeration, aimed at quick, entertaining reads. The other three are restrained, factual headlines typical of broadsheets, which assume an audience wanting depth and analysis.

questions.stem: What is the correct order of the three redrafting stages?
choices: Proofread → rewrite → annotate
Rewrite → annotate → proofread
Annotate → proofread → rewrite
Annotate → rewrite → proofread
questions.explanation: First annotate — mark up the first draft with the changes and additions it needs. Then rewrite — produce a cleaner version guided by those notes. Proofread last: there is no point perfecting the spelling of sentences you are about to rewrite, so error-checking always comes after the content is settled.

questions.stem: A student writes in a complaint letter to the council: 'The bins ain't been emptied for ages and it's doing my head in.' Which rewrite keeps the meaning but fixes the register?
choices: 'Your rubbish collection is a disgrace and heads should roll.'
'The refuse collection has not taken place for several weeks, causing considerable inconvenience to residents.'
'The bins have not been emptied for ages, which is extremely frustrating.'
'I am writing to inform you that the bins ain't been emptied.'
questions.explanation: The correct version replaces slang ('ain't', 'ages', 'doing my head in') with precise, impersonal formal language while keeping the same facts. The first option adds aggressive new meaning; the third keeps the vague informal 'ages' and the emotional 'frustrating'; the fourth keeps 'ain't' inside an otherwise formal frame — a classic register clash.

questions.stem: A travel article aims to inform AND entertain. Which combination of techniques best achieves both?
choices: A complete itinerary listing every place visited, in order
Statistics about the country's economy and population
Sensory description of the place mixed with facts and a personal anecdote
A detailed account of the writer's feelings about the journey
questions.explanation: Sensory detail (sights, sounds, smells) entertains by making the reader feel present; facts about the place inform; anecdote adds voice and humour. A full itinerary and economic statistics inform without entertaining, while feelings alone entertain without informing — travel writing works by selection and blend, not exhaustiveness.

questions.stem: An argument paragraph reads: 'Homework is a terrible idea. It is boring and unfair. Everyone hates it. It should be banned immediately.' Which revision would most strengthen the argument?
choices: Add a supporting fact or example and explain how it proves the point
Add more emotive adjectives such as 'dreadful' and 'outrageous'
Repeat the main claim at the end of the paragraph for emphasis
Start every sentence with 'Also' to link the points together
questions.explanation: The paragraph is a bare claim plus assertions — it states opinions but offers no evidence. A real argument needs a supporting statement (a fact, statistic, example or expert view) plus reasoning that connects it to the claim. More emotive language just inflates unsupported opinion, repetition adds nothing new, and mechanical 'Also' connectives don't create logical links.

questions.stem: Choose the best connective: 'The new leisure centre will cost the council £2 million. ___, it will create forty jobs and provide the district's only public pool.'
choices: Therefore
Consequently
Similarly
That said
questions.explanation: The first clause raises a negative (cost) and the second answers it with positives, so the relationship is concession — 'That said' (like 'however') signals the turn. 'Therefore' and 'Consequently' wrongly claim the jobs were caused by the cost; 'Similarly' suggests the clauses make the same kind of point. Contrast connectives work in either direction: bad news first, then good.
